newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Honduran judge stops extradition of Haitian colonel.
newsitem.headline: Honduran judge stops extradition of Haitian colonel.

text.p: A Honduran judge on Wednesday threw out a request to extradite Haiti's ex-police chief Col. Joseph Michel Francois to the United States to face drug-running charges.

"The judge in the case has acquitted my client and thrown out the extradition request to the United States. The judge did not find him guilty of any of the charges leveled against him," the colonel's attorney Francisco Lagos told reporters.
Francois, police chief of Haiti's capital Port-au-Prince under the 1991-1994 military government, was arrested on March 7 in San Pedro Sula, a Honduran city north of the capital.

Francois, 39, celebrated the verdict. "You have to be happy if you are innocent," he said at the courthouse. "They (the United States) have not presented the proof to back up the accusations that they made against me."
The U.S. Embassy in Honduras, which wanted to take Francois to Miami for trial, has three days to present an appeal or he could be released from custody.

"My sentence favours Francois and now the U.S. Embassy has three days to present an appeal. If it is not presented by the end of that period I will proceed to order that Francois be released," Judge Marco Alvarado told reporters.
It was not clear whether the United States would appeal.

The U.S. Attorney General's indictment against Francois said he placed Haiti's military and political hierarchy under his control to ship thousands of pounds of cocaine and heroin to the United States in league with Colombian drug barons.

Francois is believed to have been the mastermind behind the September 1991 coup that toppled President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. He became the capital's police chief and created a network of plainclothes policemen known as "attaches" who instigated a reign of terror against opponents of the regime.
He fled to Honduras in April 1996 after winning political asylum there along with the ex-mayor of Port-au-Prince Frank Rommaind.
